summary: This best current practice says native apps should make OAuth 2.0 authorization requests only through external user agents, mainly the user's browser, and not through embedded web views. It explains the security and usability reasons and how apps and servers can follow it.

eli5.summary: When an app asks you to log in, it is safer to open your trusted browser than a window the app controls, because the app could peek at your password.

questions: how should native apps use oauth
why not use embedded webviews for oauth
what redirect uri should a native app use
is pkce required for native apps
subtitle: Why native apps should send people to the real browser to sign in with OAuth, and how the result gets back to the app.

tldr.problem: Native apps often showed the OAuth login page inside an embedded web view, which lets the app copy passwords and cookies and forces users to sign in again in every app.
tldr.mechanism: The app opens the authorization request in an external user-agent, usually the browser, and gets the answer back through a redirect URI that the operating system hands to the app, with PKCE protecting the authorization code.
tldr.outcome: This is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 6749. Native apps MUST NOT use embedded user-agents for OAuth, and authorization servers have to support three kinds of redirect URI.

today: RFC 8252 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 212) that updates RFC 6749, and it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC in the metadata for this site. Its main rule, no embedded user-agents for native app OAuth, stays the practice it documents.

sections.title: Browser Instead of Embedded Web View
sections.content:
Section 9 of OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) describes two ways for a native app to reach the authorization endpoint: an embedded user-agent and an external user-agent. This document requires that native apps use only external user-agents, such as the user's browser.

The practice is also known as the AppAuth pattern, after open-source libraries that implement it. A native app here means an app installed on the device. Apps built with web technology but distributed as native apps count as native apps too.

Embedded user-agents were common, but they have drawbacks: the host app can copy the user's credentials and cookies, and the user has to authenticate from scratch in every app.
sections.eli5: An app can show a login page in its own little window, or it can send you to your real browser. This guide says to always use the real browser.

sections.title: External and Embedded User-Agents
sections.content:
An external user-agent is a separate entity or security domain from the app, so the app cannot read its cookie storage or inspect and change the page content. An embedded user-agent is hosted by the app, so the app can do all of those things. A web-view is a browser component embedded in an app and under the app's control.

An in-app browser tab sits in between in looks only. It is a real browser tab shown inside the host app that keeps the full security properties and sign-in state of the browser. Where the platform supports them, apps are RECOMMENDED to use in-app browser tabs for usability.

Using the browser means the OAuth request and response are already URIs, so the OAuth protocol itself does not change. Some servers that assume every client is a confidential web client need to learn about public native clients and their redirect URIs.
sections.eli5: An external browser is a room the app cannot look into. An embedded one is a room the app built, so the app can peek at everything you do in it.

sections.title: The Authorization Flow
sections.content:
The flow uses the authorization code grant from Section 4.1 of RFC 6749. The app opens a browser tab with the authorization request. The authorization endpoint authenticates the user and obtains consent, possibly by chaining to other authentication systems. The server then issues an authorization code to the redirect URI, and the operating system passes it to the app.

The app presents the code at the token endpoint, which validates it and issues the requested tokens. The browser's existing session gives single sign-on, so the user does not have to log in again for each app unless the server's policy says so.

Public native app clients MUST implement PKCE (RFC 7636), and authorization servers MUST support it for them. The RFC also says the implicit grant is NOT RECOMMENDED for native apps, because it cannot be protected by PKCE and its access tokens cannot be refreshed without user interaction.
sections.eli5: The app sends you to the browser, you log in there, and the browser hands the app a one-time ticket. The app swaps that ticket for the real key.

sections.title: Three Ways to Get the Answer Back
sections.content:
Authorization servers MUST offer at least three redirect URI options to native apps, and apps may use whichever suits them.

  • Private-use URI scheme: the app registers a scheme with the operating system, which launches the app when a URI with that scheme is loaded. The scheme MUST be based on a domain name the app controls, in reverse order, such as com.example.app. An example is com.example.app:/oauth2redirect/example-provider, with only a single slash after the scheme. A scheme such as myapp would not meet the requirement.
  • Claimed https URI: some operating systems let an app claim https URIs in domains it controls. The operating system guarantees the app's identity to the authorization server, so native apps SHOULD prefer this option where possible.
  • Loopback interface: apps that can open a port without special permissions use http://127.0.0.1:{port}/{path} or http://[::1]:{port}/{path}. The server MUST allow any port in the request, and clients are RECOMMENDED to try both IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.eli5: There are three mailboxes the answer can be dropped in: a special name only your app answers to, a street address the phone knows belongs to your app, or a little door on your own computer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Code interception is the main worry. Several apps can usually register the same private-use scheme, so it is unclear which one gets the authorization code. PKCE makes an intercepted code useless: the client sends a hash of a secret verifier in the request and must present the unhashed verifier when redeeming the code. Servers SHOULD reject native app requests that do not use PKCE.

Other requirements and recommendations:

  • Native apps are public clients and MUST be registered as such. Servers MUST require the complete redirect URI, including the path, to match exactly, except for the port on loopback redirects.
  • Servers SHOULD reject any private-use scheme that does not contain a period.
  • Shared secrets built into an app are not confidential, so requiring them is NOT RECOMMENDED.
  • Apps are RECOMMENDED to put a high-entropy random value in the state parameter and reject responses that do not match a pending request.
  • To block authorization server mix-up, each server the app uses MUST get its own redirect URI, and the app MUST verify that the response arrived on exactly the URI it stored.
  • For loopback, using the IP literal is preferred and localhost is NOT RECOMMENDED, and clients should listen only on the loopback interface and open the port only during the request.

Embedded user-agents are unsafe because the host app can record keystrokes, auto-submit forms to skip consent and copy session cookies. They also have no address bar or certificate display, which trains users to type credentials without checking the site.
sections.eli5: The risk is that a sneaky app grabs the ticket meant for another app. PKCE is a secret handshake only the real app knows, so a stolen ticket is no good.

sections.title: Platform Notes and Server Checklist
sections.content:
Appendix A is a checklist for OAuth servers that support native apps. They must support private-use scheme redirects, https redirects for public native clients, loopback IP redirects and PKCE, and must not assume that a native client can keep a secret.

Appendix B is non-normative and covers iOS, Android, Windows, macOS and Linux. It names in-app browser tab features (SFSafariViewController on iOS, Custom Tabs on Android) and says desktop apps typically use a loopback redirect. On Windows, apps SHOULD set SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE on the loopback socket. On Linux, apps SHOULD NOT set SO_REUSEPORT or SO_REUSEADDR. The RFC notes these details were accurate at publication but will likely change, and the generic principles take precedence.
sections.eli5: Each kind of phone or computer has its own way of doing this, so the guide lists a few. The main rules stay the same everywhere.
